analysis.one_liner: Adds dental care, including cleanings, fillings, root canals, and dentures, to Medicare.
analysis.headline: Both House committees approved it and it was placed on the House calendar in January 2020, but the House never voted and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Traditional Medicare has excluded almost all dental care since 1965, so seniors and people with disabilities pay out of pocket for cleanings, fillings, root canals, and dentures. This bill would have added dental and oral health services to Medicare Part B: two exams and two cleanings a year, plus basic and major treatments and a set of dentures once every five years. Coverage of major work was phased in slowly, paying 10% of the cost in 2022 and rising to 50% by 2026, so patients would have still paid a large share of expensive dental work in the early years.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 60 million seniors and disabled Americans on Medicare would gain dental coverage they currently lack. Today they pay dentists directly out of pocket, and untreated dental problems drive other health problems in older adults. Dentists would also gain a new pool of paying patients who currently skip care because they cannot afford it.

how_it_helps.text: Medicare Part B would cover preventive and screening dental services: oral exams, dental cleanings, x-rays, and fluoride treatments, capped at two exams and two cleanings per 12-month period.

Basic treatments, which may include basic tooth restorations, periodontal services, tooth extractions, and oral disease management, would be covered at 80% of the Medicare payment rate, leaving a 20% patient share.

Major treatments, which may include crowns, bridges, dental implants, and root canals, would be phased in at 10% payment in 2022, rising 10 percentage points each year to 50% by 2026, with Medicare covering half the cost thereafter.
Medicare would pay for dentures, which it has excluded outright until now, once every five years per person, fitted by written order of a doctor or oral health professional.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare's federal budget: the bill funds implementation through transfers from the federal Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund, which is financed by taxpayer premiums and general revenue. Dentists would face Medicare payment rates for dental work that is currently billed at whatever the market bears, and seniors would still pay coinsurance and the full cost of major work in the early years of the phase-in.

drawbacks.text: The bill adds a significant new permanent entitlement with no dedicated new revenue: implementation would be funded through transfers from the Medicare Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund, raising the pressure on a fund already projected to face shortfalls.

Coverage of expensive major work is phased in slowly: Medicare would pay only 10% of the cost of crowns, implants, and root canals in 2022 and just 50% even after the phase-in ends in 2026, so patients would bear the rest out of pocket.
Dentures are limited to once every five years per person, and other services are subject to frequency limits set by the Secretary, leaving gaps for people with heavy dental needs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to seniors is real and large: dental care is one of the biggest out-of-pocket medical costs older Americans face, and untreated dental disease worsens other health conditions. The design has honest weaknesses: the slow phase-in means the people who most need crowns, implants, and dentures would still pay most of those costs in the early years, and the new spending would draw on a trust fund without new dedicated financing. A stronger version would have covered major work faster and identified how to pay for it. Even so, the core expansion would have helped millions of people afford care they currently skip or forgo.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared both House committees with voice votes and was placed on the House calendar in January 2020, but no floor vote was ever scheduled, and it died when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robin Kelly introduced the bill on October 11, 2019, after a House Health Subcommittee hearing on the issue, with Rep. Steven Horsford as the original cosponsor.
Ten House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The Ways and Means Committee reported the bill favorably in December 2019 and the Energy and Commerce Committee followed in January 2020, both by voice vote.
The bill was placed on the Union Calendar on January 24, 2020, Calendar No. 303, but the House never took it up for a vote, and it died at the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Dentists and other dental providers keep collecting payment directly from seniors out of pocket, and private Medicare Advantage insurers keep dental coverage as a selling point for pulling seniors out of traditional Medicare. Seniors needing dental care remain where they were: paying out of pocket or going without.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Dental providers and Medicare Advantage insurers

sides.party_line_note: All ten cosponsors were House Democrats, no Republicans signed on, and the bill never reached a recorded floor vote where partisan splits could be counted.

industries.note: The bill would make Medicare a paying customer for dental care that seniors currently skip or pay for out of pocket, and it exempts dentists from certain Medicare physician payment rules. Dentists gain patients and revenue; seniors gain access, so their interests run together here.

Dental benefits are a key marketing tool private Medicare Advantage plans use to attract seniors away from traditional Medicare; adding dental to traditional Medicare would remove that advantage. The bill does not regulate them directly, but it erodes one of their competitive draws.

Medicare would pay for dentures for the first time, creating demand, but the bill routes dentures through Medicare's competitive acquisition program, which puts suppliers in price competition and exempts only dentures fitted by a practitioner's own patients.
